claims.text: High-entropy alloys consist of five or more metallic elements in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The as-prepared nanoparticles are homogeneous, random, single-phase solid solutions without detectable chemical ordering or phase separation.
Structural and chemical stability is governed by competition between configurational entropy and ordering enthalpy from pairwise interactions.
High configurational entropy favors a chemically disordered solid-solution phase, especially at elevated temperature.
At lower temperatures, favorable pairwise ordering enthalpy can overcome the configurational-entropy contribution and promote chemical ordering.
Atomic-size mismatch produces severe lattice distortion in the nanoparticles.
Reduced atomic diffusivity kinetically hinders chemical ordering and phase separation.
HEA nanoparticles can retain structurally similar single-solid-solution states over 573–1000 K.
Near 1923 K, the nanoparticles will remain nearly unchanged and single-phase.
High-temperature exposure will cause only minor shifts in lattice parameters.
Near 473 K, slight chemical ordering or incipient phase segregation may occur if ordering enthalpy becomes competitive.
An inert or controlled atmosphere prevents oxidation during temperature cycling.
Slightly skewing the elemental ratios will reduce lattice distortion.
A composition with reduced lattice distortion should order more readily than the equiatomic comparison.
Critical ordering temperatures and the relative magnitudes of ordering enthalpy and configurational entropy may vary with small composition changes.
Temperature-independent retention of a homogeneous single phase or absence of a difference after modifying lattice distortion would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism and prediction make low-temperature ordering conditional and explicitly allow lattice-distortion-induced kinetic hindrance to preserve a homogeneous phase. The falsification rule nevertheless treats homogeneous behavior at all temperatures as falsifying, even though that result could be explained by the proposed kinetic hindrance.
